sections.h2: Three ways to remove a tenant in Arkansas
sections.html:
A landlord can use a civil lawsuit called unlawful detainer, a case under the Residential Landlord-Tenant Act of 2007, or a criminal charge for refusing to leave. Most owners begin with one of the first two.

Unlawful detainer is defined in Ark. Code § 18-60-304. A tenant commits it by staying past the end of a lease, by ignoring a written demand to leave, by skipping rent and then refusing to go after three days' written notice, by letting the home become unsafe or unhealthy, or by allowing a common nuisance. It is the most common type of eviction in the state.

The Landlord-Tenant Act route starts at § 18-17-901. The landlord or an agent files in district court when rent is not paid when due or demanded, when the occupancy term has ended, or when the rental agreement has been broken. On a residential lease, rent that stays unpaid five days past the due date counts as legal notice that eviction proceedings can begin.

How much notice a landlord owes depends on why the tenancy is ending. Match the notice to the lease and to the statute that fits your facts, because the periods differ.

SituationNotice or waiting periodStatute
Rent unpaid, unlawful detainerThree days' written notice to quit§ 18-60-304(3)
Rent unpaid, Landlord-Tenant ActLandlord may terminate if rent is not paid within five days of the due date§ 18-17-701(b)
Other lease violationWritten notice with a termination date at least 14 days after receipt, if not fixed§ 18-17-701(a)
Week-to-week tenancyWritten notice at least 7 days before the end date§ 18-17-704(a)
Month-to-month tenancyWritten notice at least 30 days before the end date§ 18-17-704(b)
Criminal failure to vacateTen days' written notice to vacate§ 18-16-101(b)

In plain terms, the civil clock is at least three days for unpaid rent, at least 14 days for other violations, and at least one month to end a month-to-month tenancy. A landlord may also end a lease for any reason by giving one rental period's notice on an oral lease, or the notice a written lease calls for.

sections.h2: What happens after the notice runs out
sections.html:
If the tenant is still in the house, the landlord files a complaint with the court. The case then moves through a short series of steps.

  • Service. The tenant must receive the summons and complaint through a process server or by certified mail.
  • Five days to object. A tenant who receives a summons has five days to object in writing to the court clerk. With no objection, the county sheriff can remove the tenant.
  • Order to vacate or show cause. If the complaint carries an affidavit from someone who knows why eviction is sought, the court issues an order to vacate, or to appear and show cause, within ten calendar days after service. A written answer counts as an appearance.
  • Hearing. If the tenant appears, the judge hears both sides. A judgment for the tenant lets the tenant stay until the tenancy ends by agreement or law, rent goes unpaid, or another eviction case succeeds (§ 18-17-908).
  • Writ of possession. When the landlord wins, the clerk issues a writ and the sheriff serves it. The tenant then has 24 hours to leave. The sheriff carries it out under § 18-60-310, as § 18-17-913 directs.

These are minimums. The court calendar sets the hearing date, and no statute fixes a total number of days from first notice to move-out.

sections.h2: The criminal failure to vacate charge
sections.html:
It is a misdemeanor when a tenant willfully refuses to leave after ten days' written notice from the landlord, the landlord's agent or the landlord's attorney. The rule is in Ark. Code § 18-16-101.

The same section says a renter who fails to pay rent when due forfeits the right to keep living in the dwelling. A conviction carries a fine of $1 to $25 per offense, and each day of willful holding over after the notice expires counts as its own offense.

sections.h2: Can a landlord change the locks or shut off utilities?
sections.html:
No. A landlord needs a court order and a writ of possession carried out by the sheriff. Self-help is off the table.

  • Changing the locks is a self-help eviction.
  • Taking out the tenant's belongings, doors or windows is self-help too.
  • So is cutting off water, power or other utilities.

One exception applies: the same acts can be lawful once the tenant has moved out or the landlord reasonably believes the property is abandoned. A tenant who is locked out can sue for forcible entry, and the court may restore access and award damages, costs and attorney's fees. The landlord can counterclaim to evict in that same case, since a lockout alone gives the tenant no right to stay when a legal ground for eviction exists.

When a lease ends, voluntarily or not, whatever the tenant leaves behind is treated as abandoned. The landlord may dispose of it as he or she sees fit, and the tenant has no recourse. Property left on the premises is also subject to a landlord's lien for sums the tenant agreed to pay.

Where law enforcement carries out the eviction, items the tenant cannot take are removed and stored at the tenant's expense. If the tenant moves out first and leaves things behind, the landlord can treat them as abandoned and throw them away or sell them.

sections.h2: Can a tenant withhold rent over repairs?
sections.html:
No. Section 18-17-502 bars a tenant from offsetting or withholding rent for an alleged or actual breach of the implied quality standards, and nothing in the chapter excuses a tenant from paying rent.

On leases entered into or renewed after November 1, 2021, the statute implies these basics: hot and cold running water, electricity, potable water, working sanitary sewer and plumbing, a functioning roof and building envelope, and heating and air conditioning if the home had them when the lease was signed. When the unit falls short, the tenant sends written notice. If rent is current and the landlord has not fixed the problem within 30 calendar days, the tenant's sole remedy is to end the lease without penalty and get back any recoverable security deposit.

Little Rock adds minimum housing standards for privately owned rentals with two or more dwellings, including a safe roof that does not leak. Report problems to the Department of Housing and Neighborhood Programs at 500 West Markham Street, Suite 120W, or call (501) 371-6825.

Under § 18-17-701(c), a landlord can recover actual damages, seek injunctive relief, and obtain a judgment or an eviction in circuit or district court without posting bond.

Attorney's fees are possible when a lawyer represents the landlord. They are available if nonpayment of rent is not in good faith, and for other willful noncompliance. On a holdover, § 18-17-704 allows fees when the tenant is not holding over in good faith. A willful violation can add up to three months of periodic rent or twice the actual damages, whichever is greater.

sections.h2: Evicting a tenant and selling the house
sections.html:
The sale and the eviction run on separate tracks. The statutes control who has the right to possession, and none of them ends a tenancy because the house sold. Check the lease terms and talk to a lawyer before you promise a buyer that the house will be vacant.

A few practical points connect the two. A landlord may decline to renew a lease for any reason except discriminatory ones covered by the Fair Housing Act. A month-to-month tenant must get 30 days' written notice. A cash buyer can be asked up front whether it will take the house with the tenant still inside, which avoids waiting on a court calendar.

What to line up before you list a rented house:

  • The lease, any renewal and every notice you have served.
  • Rent records showing what is paid and what is late.
  • Copies of any court filings, so the title company can see where a case stands.

Paperwork follows the sale as well. The state real property transfer tax is $3.30 per $1,000 of consideration on transactions above $100, shown on the deed through a transfer stamp. Owners should also tell the assessor when a house changes from owner-occupied to rental, because the homestead credit applies only to a principal residence.

faqs.q: How long does an Arkansas eviction take?
faqs.a: No statute sets a total. Notice runs from three days to 30 days, a tenant has five days to object, a show-cause order allows up to ten days to appear, and a tenant served with a writ has 24 hours. A contested case adds a hearing date chosen by the court.

faqs.q: Is eviction a crime in Arkansas?
faqs.a: Only the failure to vacate charge is criminal. Under § 18-16-101, a tenant who willfully stays after ten days' written notice commits a misdemeanor with a fine of $1 to $25 per offense, and each day counts separately.

faqs.q: Can a landlord evict without going to court?
faqs.a: No. The landlord needs a court order, and the sheriff carries out the writ of possession. Changing locks, removing doors or windows, or cutting utilities are illegal self-help unless the tenant has left or the property is reasonably believed abandoned.

faqs.q: Does a pending eviction stop me from selling the house?
faqs.a: No statute bars a sale while a case is open. The lease and the buyer's terms decide what happens to the tenant, so ask an Arkansas attorney before you sign a contract that promises vacant possession.

faqs.q: Where can a tenant find free legal help with an eviction?
faqs.a: Call Legal Aid of Arkansas at 1-800-952-9243. Tenants who qualify get free help.
